---
title: "P2 — Water, minerals and transport"
---

## The question

How does water reach a leaf several metres above soil, and why can salt make
water harder to obtain from wet soil? Explain water potential, root uptake,
xylem transport and stomatal regulation. Connect mineral nutrition to root and
shoot function, using units and compartments carefully.

## Water moves down a potential gradient

**Water potential**, Ψ, expresses water's chemical potential relative to a
reference in pressure units. Here we use megapascals, MPa. Net passive movement
occurs from higher to lower potential when a pathway is available. Less-negative
values are higher: −0.2 MPa exceeds −0.8 MPa. Total potential determines
direction, not solute concentration alone when pressure differs.

For a small hydrated-cell system we often simplify to:

$$\Psi = \Psi_s + \Psi_p.$$

Solute potential Ψs becomes more negative as dissolved-particle concentration
increases. Ψp is pressure potential. A fuller account includes gravity and
matric effects, important for tall plants, soil and drying tissues. Omitting
them is a stated approximation for this small system.

A cell with Ψs = −0.9 MPa and Ψp = +0.4 MPa has Ψ = −0.5 MPa. Surroundings
at −0.2 MPa initially favour inward movement. As water enters, wall resistance
can raise pressure and dilution can change solute potential. Initial values do
not remain fixed. At equilibrium there is no net movement, although molecular
exchange continues. Positive turgor can coexist with negative total Ψ.

## Roots contain pathways and selective barriers

Water crosses tissues by apoplastic, symplastic and transmembrane routes.
Aquaporins increase membrane permeability in appropriate states; they do not
pump water uphill. Permeability affects how readily movement occurs, while the
potential difference explains passive direction.

The endodermis surrounds the vascular region. Its Casparian strip restricts an
uninterrupted wall-space route into the stele, helping ensure substances
encounter selective membranes. Developing roots acquire additional barriers.
Consequently, an entire root is not a uniform filter with constant permeability.

Roots take up mineral ions through channels and carriers. Plasma-membrane
proton pumps use ATP to establish electrochemical gradients. Coupling to those
gradients can drive uptake of other solutes against their own gradients.
This is distinct from actively pumping water. Root respiration supports many
uptake processes, so waterlogging can impair mineral nutrition when oxygen is
limited even though water is abundant.

## Evaporation connects leaves to xylem tension

Water evaporates from wet internal wall surfaces and vapour diffuses towards
the atmosphere. Negative pressure can develop in the xylem water. Cohesion and
adhesion help transmit tension through the conducting pathway. The
**cohesion–tension mechanism** supports long-distance movement without a pump
at each height.

Xylem water columns can become discontinuous through cavitation and embolism.
Hydraulic efficiency and vulnerability depend on conduit structure and
conditions. Root pressure contributes in some situations but is not a general
explanation for supplying tall transpiring tree crowns.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  soil[Soil water: relatively high potential] --> root[Root pathways and endodermis]
  root --> xyl[Water-filled xylem under tension]
  xyl --> wall[Wet leaf cell walls]
  wall --> spaces[Leaf air spaces]
  spaces --> stoma[Stomatal pore]
  stoma --> air[Atmosphere: low water potential]
  signal[Guard-cell signals] --> stoma
```

This original schematic represents a transpiring plant with a favourable
soil-to-air gradient. Values and flow rates change with conditions. It shows
neither all anatomical routes nor a guarantee of an intact water column.

Transpiration depends on energy, humidity, air movement, temperature and leaf
area. A larger vapour pressure deficit can favour water loss if conductance
is maintained. A chamber changes the leaf environment. Document these factors
before attributing a difference entirely to plant genotype or treatment.

## Stomata regulate carbon gain and water loss

A stoma is a pore bordered by guard cells. Ion transport changes guard-cell
osmotic conditions, water movement and turgor; wall geometry converts these
changes into pore movement. Light, CO2, water status and signals influence the
response. Opening assists carbon acquisition while increasing vapour loss.
Closing conserves water but can reduce carbon gain and evaporative cooling.

Abscisic acid, ABA, participates in drought signalling and stomatal closure.
It influences ion-channel activity and other cellular processes rather than
physically plugging a pore. Channel responses and subsequent growth changes
operate on different timescales. Cuticle, rooting depth, hydraulic conductance
and leaf area also matter. Similar stomatal conductance therefore does not
guarantee identical whole-plant water status.

## Essential minerals have specific roles

An essential element is required to complete the life cycle and has a role
another element cannot simply replace. “Macro” and “micro” indicate typical
required quantities rather than importance. Nitrogen contributes to amino
acids and nucleotides; phosphorus to phosphorylated metabolites and nucleic
acids; potassium to osmotic regulation and enzyme activity. Magnesium is part
of chlorophyll, and iron participates in electron-transfer systems.

A yellow leaf does not uniquely diagnose one deficiency. Age, symptom pattern,
element mobility, root condition and pH all matter. A readily remobilised
element may leave old tissues to support new growth, making old leaves useful
diagnostic clues. Nevertheless, symptoms require verification. Excess can also
be harmful, and total soil content is not the same as root availability.

Mycorrhizal fungi can extend access to resources while receiving plant carbon.
Nitrogen-fixing symbioses also connect resource acquisition to carbon supply.
Benefits vary with host, partner and conditions. “Microbes improve growth” is
an incomplete prediction unless the limiting resource and context are stated.

## Drought and salinity have overlapping effects

Drying soil lowers water availability and can reduce hydraulic connectivity.
Salts lower the solute (osmotic) potential and can cause ion toxicity or nutrient imbalance.
Compatible-solute accumulation can contribute to osmotic adjustment but carries
costs. Conserving water through closure can reduce carbon gain. A plant may
survive a treatment without maintaining growth or reproduction.

Consider soil at −0.1 MPa versus saline soil solution at −0.6 MPa. A root cell
initially at −0.4 MPa has a favourable inward gradient in the first setting
and an outward one in the second, all else equal. Real compartments respond.
The calculation identifies the initial challenge rather than final yield.

## Match measurement and claim

A pot loses water through soil evaporation as well as transpiration. A soil
cover or appropriate unplanted control can help distinguish them. Five leaves
from one pot do not supply five independent pots when watering was assigned
to pots. Describe measurements at their actual level before choosing an
analysis. Advanced statistics cannot manufacture independent treatment units.
